rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a story and an attractive trap: it explicitly refuses "Warby Parker's expansion creates hundreds of optometrist jobs nationwide," while B walks into the same hole with "Warby Parker's retail expansion means a large new employer of optometrists." A's line "Warby Parker got profitable — now it's spending on stores, and won't say what the exams earn" gives a markets reporter a real tension. B has good bones, but it pads the set with an employment story it cannot prove.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker was the canonical example of that thesis" is useful context, but it is not in the supplied update. Source it or soften it.
"pharmacy chains' fight to reinvent the front of store" imports an outside trend that was not supplied. It may be true, but this angle needs evidence before it leaves the room.
"funding a 40-store buildout" slightly overreads the update. The facts say Warby is profitable and opening stores, not how the buildout is funded.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker's retail expansion means a large new employer of optometrists" is the bad kind of confident. The update says optometrist-staffed exams, not direct employment or large hiring.
"hiring will follow the store opening schedule" is invented. Maybe true, maybe not; that is exactly why it should not be stated as fact.

"where Americans can get optical care without visiting a specialty store" overstates the pharmacy pilot. The update says Warby will sell glasses through a pharmacy chain, not provide exams or optical care there.
"the DTC survival argument in one announcement" is a tidy phrase doing too much work. Profitability plus expansion is a signal, not a proved survival thesis.
